source_read: PMC HTML (saved text of PMC11076881, published version), read start to end: abstract, Introduction and its epidemiology subsection, haemorrhagic-stroke sections (vignette, epidemiology, pathophysiology, treatment and outcomes), ischaemic-stroke sections (vignette, epidemiology, pathophysiology, treatment), Diagnostic challenges and management, Conclusion, author contributions, funding and conflict statements, publisher's note, all 106 references. Figures 1-5 are images absent from the text (only their legends were read). The 'Author information' and 'Article notes' panels are collapsed in the save, so affiliations, dates and editor/reviewer names could not be checked.

design.note: narrative-review is right: no methods, search, eligibility criteria or appraisal; two illustrative vignettes.

key_findings.note: Hemorrhagic › Epidemiology & characteristics ¶1: 2-5 times (refs 11, 37), 6.2 vs 20.8 per 100,000 person-years (Huang), over 80% of case reports and series haemorrhagic (ref 13, Lappin 2017). The card's note on OR 4.95 and HR 2.09 comes from Lappin et al. (2017), not from this paper, and was not checked in this reading.

key_findings.correction: Attribution is narrower than the source. The review cites refs 13, 38 and 39 (Lappin 2017; Swor 2019; Zhu 2020) for younger age, better pre-stroke function and fewer comorbidities, refs 13 and 39 for male predominance, and ref 39 (Zhu 2020) alone for lower hypertension and antithrombotic use and higher smoking; only the smoking difference is described as significant. Location (Epidemiology & characteristics ¶2-3) is right.

key_findings.note: Epidemiology & characteristics ¶4 (usually aneurysmal; younger, refs 44-45; no consensus on vasospasm and Hunt-Hess; 23 patients, type and location not different, ref 46) and Pathophysiology of hemorrhagic stroke, last paragraph (aspect ratio larger).

key_findings.correction: Content is exact (14 people with intravenous polysubstance use, 12 reporting methamphetamine, 1 exclusively; 4 fatal cases, 2 confirmed and 1 possible; monkeys; over 400 San Francisco deaths; 38 Australian fatal strokes; invoke rarely and with skepticism). It is in Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶4, counting text paragraphs. The card's ¶5 counts the Figure 2 legend as a paragraph; under that count a reader of the PMC page lands on the chronic-hypertension paragraph. The Brecht card in this batch counts text paragraphs only, so the convention should be standardised.

Content confirmed (no change in mean arterial pressure in small-animal studies, ref 65; white-matter hyperintensities independent of other cardiovascular risk factors, ref 66). Location is Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶5 by text paragraphs; the card's ¶6 counts the Figure 2 legend.

key_findings.note: Last paragraph of the haemorrhagic pathophysiology section: 62 patients, median 5.5 mm, mean 6.3 mm (Noblett); meta-analytic mean 6.1 mm (ref 74). 'Size alone does not show higher rupture risk' is a fair paraphrase of the authors' point about the limits of size.

key_findings.correction: Two fixes. (1) 'A larger fall from pre-stroke mRS' should read a larger worsening (increase) in mRS from pre-stroke to discharge; mRS rises with disability, so 'fall' reads as improvement. (2) The review cites that point to refs 38 and 39 together (Swor 2019 and Zhu 2020), not to Zhu 2020 alone. The rest is confirmed at Therapeutic considerations & outcomes in meth-related hemorrhagic stroke ¶2 (n=41 vs n=61; the review itself misprints 'IV hypertensive agents', which the card rightly renders as antihypertensives).

key_findings.note: Same section ¶3. Recomputed geometric midpoints: sqrt(1.03 x 24) = 4.97 (consistent with OR 5); sqrt(1.2 x 30) = 6.0, so the card's asymmetry note for the 3-year OR 7.2 is right.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed (10/30 ventricular thrombi; QTc prolongation 27% of 158; 86% higher risk of atrial fibrillation diagnosis; endocarditis even left/right with stimulants, 75% methamphetamine, versus 66% right-sided with opioids). Location is Pathophysiology of methamphetamine-related ischemic stroke ¶2-3 by text paragraphs; the card's ¶3-4 counts the Figure 5 legend.

key_findings.note: Therapeutic considerations in methamphetamine ischemic stroke ¶1-3. The review's 'only one case report' of thrombolysis refers to the literature; its own second vignette also received thrombolysis.
Diagnostic challenges and management ¶1-2; 29/379 = 7.65%, rounds to 7.7%.
Both vignettes as stated; spasm was seen with instrumentation of the internal carotid artery and in MCA branches after reperfusion. The card rightly omits the treatment doses given in the vignettes.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: Introduction › Epidemiology ¶2 gives 39 + 33 + 29 + 8 = 109%, and calls 39% the majority.

Introduction › Epidemiology ¶3 attributes 50.9% women to people who used methamphetamine in 2015-2019 (ref 29). The Han et al. card's key finding 0, confirmed by round 1's second reader, gives 50.9% as the weighted share of women in the whole 195,711-person NSDUH sample, so the misattribution is supported.

The review's side is confirmed (Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5: up to 6.5 times, ref 9, Kaku & Lowenstein 1990). The comparison figures attributed to Lappin et al. (2017, Table 3: 6.5 ischaemic, 11.7 haemorrhagic) come from another paper and could not be checked in this reading.
Ischemic pathophysiology ¶2 cites ref 85 for the 86% figure; ref 85 is Gawałko & Sanders, Eur Heart J 2022;43:4943-5, an editorial by title and 3-page length.

Confirmed in this source: the sentence (ischemic pathophysiology ¶2, last sentence) cites refs 12 and 86-88, and the titles of 86-88 (a case of infarction with normal coronaries, an echocardiographic comparison, a study of binge administration) do not concern severity of use as a predictor. Not checkable here: that the corresponding sentence in Kevil et al. (2019) carries no citation, and that ref 88 is a rat study (its title names no species).

Refs 92 (Chapman 2022) and 94 (Loewenhardt 2013) are titled 'amphetamine-induced'; the text describes methamphetamine use. The same title check applies to ref 62 (Rumbaugh 1971, 'amphetamine abuse in the experimental animal', described as a methamphetamine study in monkeys) and ref 60 (Bostwick 1981, 'amphetamine induced cerebral vasculitis').

Confirmed in this source: the 2-5 times figure is worded as intracerebral haemorrhage (Epidemiology & characteristics ¶1) with no intervals or adjustment, and ref 37's title concerns amphetamines or cocaine. Not checkable here: that both estimates are for haemorrhagic stroke generally, which rests on Lappin et al. (2017).

risk_of_bias.note: Wrong instrument for the design. The card is labelled narrative-review but is appraised with AMSTAR 2 (overall critically low). Under METHODS §5.3 a narrative review uses the editors' narrative-review checklist (instrument 'none-applicable'); scripts/rob_vocab.py flags this mismatch. Proposed checklist judgments: systematic search and explicit selection = high (no methods, search or criteria); appraisal of the cited studies = some concerns (informal appraisal of ICD-coded hospital cohorts, small aneurysmal-haemorrhage outcome studies, the 1970 vasculitis series and small route-of-use numbers, but the 2-5-fold, 6.5-fold and 86% figures are passed on without design, intervals or adjustment, one via an editorial); reliance on the authors' own work = low (only the two vignettes come from the authors' centre; no cited study is by the authors as far as the reference list shows); separation of evidence from speculation = some concerns (the body labels speculation, e.g. aneurysm growth and stroke risk after stopping, but the abstract and conclusion present 'clear risk', greater disability and a rising contribution to stroke in the young as findings); balance = some concerns (the body reports null and conflicting results, but the abstract and conclusion select the adverse readings). Overall = high, the worst domain. The substance of the card's AMSTAR reasoning (unsystematic, unappraised, every number to be taken from the primary source) carries over.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right. Each listed gap was found independently: 'clear risk' in the Conclusion; abstract on rising stroke rates in the young against Introduction › Epidemiology ¶5 (trends not specific to methamphetamine); greater disability in the Conclusion against no difference in discharge function or mortality (Therapeutic considerations & outcomes ¶2); 'case studies and series' in the abstract against the cohort and database studies in the body; the attribution in both vignettes.

missed: The abstract's statement that haemorrhagic stroke is the more common methamphetamine-related stroke type rests on the share of published case reports and series (over 80% haemorrhagic, ref 13). A share of published cases reflects what gets reported, not relative incidence, and the population studies cited give relative risks, not the haemorrhagic-to-ischaemic ratio among people who use methamphetamine. The card's interpretation gap does not flag this inference; monograph wording should not say 'more common' on this basis.

The withdrawal time course, which the abstract lists as one of the review's points, is not recorded: Diagnostic challenges and management ¶5 gives an early crash of 12-24 h, a withdrawal phase of 2-4 weeks and an 'extinction phase' of up to 6-12 months with cognitive and mood changes (refs 105-106, Acheson et al. 2023 and a 2009 Cochrane review). It is second-hand and should be traced to those sources before use, but the card should record it with that caveat.
other_notes: analysis.covariates: the review's text does not call the Moon et al. association 'independent'; that word comes from the reference title (ref 45).
replication.timeline: 'ages 18-44' (Westover) and '98 published cases' (Lappin) are not in this source; they presumably come from other papers and were not checked here.

Diagnostic challenges and management ¶4 repeats Brecht & Herbeck's self-help/further-treatment association as the strongest predictor of time to relapse, without the immortal-time problem flagged on sc_brecht_2014; any monograph use of the review on continuing care inherits that caveat.

Introduction › Epidemiology ¶4 says overdose deaths involving methamphetamine with opioids 'peaked in 2021, the most recent year of data'; a peak cannot be identified in the last year of a series. Minor, and second-hand.

design_detail and funding.affiliations_note (Harborview Medical Center, University of Washington; received and accepted dates; named reviewers) could not be checked: these panels are collapsed in the saved text.
